## Why Do We Need Tools for Causal Inference?

Association is not causation. We have known how to measure associations for a long time, but most econometric models are associational. The gap between the two arises from confounding.

## Confounders

In this graph, $w$ is the treatment, $y$ the outcome, and $c_1$, $c_2$ are confounders. Both confounders affect both $w$ and $y$, so the observed association between $w$ and $y$ may reflect confounding rather than a causal effect.

```{julia}
#| label: dag1
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| message: false
#| echo: false
g = SimpleDiGraph(4)
# 1=w, 2=c1, 3=c2, 4=y
add_edge!(g, 2, 1) # c1 -> w
add_edge!(g, 2, 4) # c1 -> y
add_edge!(g, 3, 1) # c2 -> w
add_edge!(g, 3, 4) # c2 -> y
add_edge!(g, 1, 4) # w -> y

labels = ["w", "c1", "c2", "y"]
pos = [Point2f(1, 2), Point2f(2, 1), Point2f(2, 3), Point2f(3, 2)]

fig, ax, p = graphplot(g, layout=pos,
                       nlabels=labels,
                       nlabels_align=(:center, :center),
                       nlabels_distance=0.0,
                       nlabels_fontsize=16,
                       node_size=50,
                       node_color=:white,
                       node_strokewidth=2,
                       node_strokecolor=:black,
                       arrow_size=15,
                       edge_color=:black)
hidedecorations!(ax)
hidespines!(ax)
fig
```

A concrete example: income and age may both drive 401(k) participation and assets. To identify the causal effect of participation on assets, we need to control for income and age.

```{julia}
#| label: dag1-2
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| message: false
#| echo: false
g = SimpleDiGraph(4)
# 1=p401k, 2=income, 3=age, 4=assets
add_edge!(g, 2, 1) # income -> p401k
add_edge!(g, 2, 4) # income -> assets
add_edge!(g, 3, 1) # age -> p401k
add_edge!(g, 3, 4) # age -> assets
add_edge!(g, 1, 4) # p401k -> assets

labels = ["p401k", "income", "age", "assets"]
pos = [Point2f(1, 2), Point2f(2, 1), Point2f(2, 3), Point2f(3, 2)]

fig, ax, p = graphplot(g, layout=pos,
                       nlabels=labels,
                       nlabels_align=(:center, :center),
                       nlabels_distance=0.0,
                       nlabels_fontsize=16,
                       node_size=80,
                       node_color=:white,
                       node_strokewidth=2,
                       node_strokecolor=:black,
                       arrow_size=15,
                       edge_color=:black)
hidedecorations!(ax)
hidespines!(ax)
fig
```

Another example: prenatal care and maternal age may affect both smoking and birth weight. Even if smoking has no causal effect on birth weight, it will appear to because of these shared causes.

```{julia}
#| label: dag1-3
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| message: false
#| echo: false
g = SimpleDiGraph(4)
# 1=mbsmoke, 2=prenatal, 3=age, 4=bweight
add_edge!(g, 2, 1) # prenatal -> mbsmoke
add_edge!(g, 2, 4) # prenatal -> bweight
add_edge!(g, 3, 1) # age -> mbsmoke
add_edge!(g, 3, 4) # age -> bweight
add_edge!(g, 1, 4) # mbsmoke -> bweight

labels = ["mbsmoke", "prenatal", "age", "bweight"]
pos = [Point2f(1, 2), Point2f(2, 1), Point2f(2, 3), Point2f(3, 2)]

fig, ax, p = graphplot(g, layout=pos,
                       nlabels=labels,
                       nlabels_align=(:center, :center),
                       nlabels_distance=0.0,
                       nlabels_fontsize=16,
                       node_size=90,
                       node_color=:white,
                       node_strokewidth=2,
                       node_strokecolor=:black,
                       arrow_size=15,
                       edge_color=:black)
hidedecorations!(ax)
hidespines!(ax)
fig
```

## Controlled and Uncontrolled Confounders

If we can control for all confounders, correlation does imply causation. The two questions are: do we observe all confounders, and how do we control for them? In a randomized experiment neither question arises. In an observational study both do. If $c_2$ is unobserved, any estimate of the effect of $w$ on $y$ is biased.

## Potential Outcome Setup

We study causal effects through the potential outcomes (counterfactual) framework. Each unit has two potential outcomes, $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$, one for each treatment state. These are fixed before any assignment; the experiment tries to recover them.

The fundamental problem is that we never observe both: only the realized outcome $Y = WY(1) + (1-W)Y(0)$ is seen. Individual treatment effects $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ are not identifiable; only averages can be estimated.

We write $W$ for treatment assignment and $X$ for covariates.

## ATE, ATT and ATU

The standard estimands are:

$$ \tau_{ATE} = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] $$ {#eq-identification-1}

$$ \tau_{ATT} =  E[Y(1) - Y(0) | W=1] $$ {#eq-identification-2}

$$ \tau_{ATU} =  E[Y(1) - Y(0)| W=0] $$ {#eq-identification-3}

$$ \tau_{ATE} = \rho \tau_{ATT} + (1-\rho) \tau_{ATU}$$ {#eq-identification-4}

where $\rho= P(W=1)$.

## Identification: From Potential Outcome to Observed

We focus on $\tau_{ATT}$. To identify it, we need: $$ E[Y(1) | W=1]$$ {#eq-identification-5} which is easy, because we observe it.

And we need $$ E[Y(0) | W=1]$$ {#eq-identification-6}

To identify this, we'll need unconfoundedness: $$ E[Y(0) | W, X] = E[Y(0)| X] $$ {#eq-identification-7} and overlap: $$ \pi(x)= P(W=1 | X=x) < 1$$ {#eq-identification-8} (for the ATT only $\pi(x)<1$ is needed; the ATE requires $0<\pi(x)<1$).

Unconfoundedness says that within each subgroup $X=x$, treated and
control units have the same mean of $Y(0)$:
$E[Y(0)|W=1,X=x]=E[Y(0)|W=0,X=x]=E[Y|W=0,X=x]$. Averaging over the
covariate distribution of the treated,

$$ E[Y(0)| W=1] = E\big[ E[Y | W=0, X] \mid W=1 \big], $$ {#eq-identification-9}

which involves only observed data. Therefore ATT is identified:

 $$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{ATT} &=  E[Y(1) - Y(0) | W=1] \\
&= E[Y|W=1] - E\big[ E[Y | W=0, X] \mid W=1 \big]
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-identification-10}


Note the conditional-on-$X$ assumption does NOT imply the marginal
equality $E[Y(0)|W=1]=E[Y(0)|W=0]$: treated and control units have
different covariate distributions, so the adjustment over $X$ is
essential. In a randomised experiment, unconfoundedness holds without
conditioning on $X$ (i.e. $E[Y(0)|W]=E[Y(0)]$); then
$E[Y(0)|W=1]=E[Y(0)|W=0]=E[Y|W=0]$, the formula collapses to
$E[Y|W=1]-E[Y|W=0]$, and a difference-in-means estimator is
consistent.

$$ \hat{\tau}_{ATT} = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0 $$ {#eq-identification-11}

But in observational studies, most cases we cannot assume unconfoundedness. What can we do to justify unconfoundedness better?

## Unconfoundedness and Overlap

Weaker Assumptions: Unconfoundedness (conditional independence, or ignorability), stated jointly for both potential outcomes since we are after the ATE here (as opposed to the ATT case above, which only required it for $Y(0)$): $$ E[Y(d) | W, X] = E[Y(d)| X] \quad \text{for } d \in \{0,1\} $$ {#eq-identification-12} Overlap: $$ 0 < \pi(x)= P(W=1 | X=x) < 1 $$ {#eq-identification-13} SUTVA (stable unit treatment value assumption): 1. No interference between units. No spillovers. 2. Consistency. No hidden versions of treatment or control. Treatment is clearly defined.

Within each subgroup of $X=x$, W is independent of $Y(0)$. With the overlap assumption, we ensure there is a comparable control unit for each treated unit.

However, these two criteria are often contradictory: we may need more covariates to satisfy conditional independence; meanwhile, if the dimension of covariates goes high, then it's likely in some partition we don't have control units.

We need four assumptions for identification:

-   Unconfoundedness (conditional independence, or ignorability)
-   Overlap (positivity, common support)
-   No interference
-   Consistency

The last two together are SUTVA, the stable unit treatment value assumption [@rubin1980].

## Observational Data Flowchart

In observational studies, I summarise the decision what method to use for identification of causal effect:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'diagramPadding': 30}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A[Observational data Y,W,X] --> B{Unconfoundedness?}
  B --> | Yes | C{Parametric?}
  C --> | Yes | D(RA)
  C --> | Yes | E(IPW)
  C --> | Yes | F(AIPW)
  C --> | Yes | G(IPWRA)
  C --> | No | H(IF based estimators)
  C --> | No | I(TMLE)
  C --> | No | J(DoubleML)
  B --> | No | K{Panel data?}
  K --> | Yes | L{Parallel Trend?}
  L --> | Yes | M(DID)
  L --> | No | N(Synthetic Control)
  L --> | No | O(Synthetic DID)
  K --> | No | P{Instrument?}
  P --> | Yes | Q(IV or RDD)
  P --> | No | R(You are stuck!)
```
